title: Updated colorectal cancer screening recommendations: Start at 45 I UCLA Health
description:
A rise in colorectal cancer cases amongst young adults led to new national guidelines lowering the recommended screening age for colorectal cancer from age 50 to 45 (May 2021). Individuals with a family history of colorectal or high-risk conditions should consult their doctor about whether they should begin screening before age 45. Colorectal cancer screening can prevent colorectal cancer through the removal of abnormal growths or polyps. It can also help doctors detect colorectal cancers early when they are most likely curable.  

Learn more about screening options, when to screen and facts about colorectal cancer at 
https://www.uclahealth.org/colon-cancer-screening/

Presented by Folasade P. May, MD, PhD

title: What Age Should Patients Get Screened for Colorectal Cancer?
description:
Although the US Preventive Services Task Force updated its recommendation in 2021 to lower the age at which patients should begin screening for colorectal cancer to 45, the American College of Physicians continues to recommend screening starting at age 50. 

In an interview with HCPLive at the 2024 American College of Physicians (ACP) Internal Medicine Meeting in Boston, Timothy Wilt, MD, MPH, professor of medicine and public health in the division of general internal medicine at the Minneapolis VA Health Care System, explained the potential benefits versus harms of screening at different ages.

“ACP believes and looks at the evidence and says that the best balance of benefits and harms is beginning screening at age 50 and that clinicians should consider recommending against not screening at age 45 because it would be a better benefit by allocating resources and screening decisions to those at greatest risk and with greatest certainty,” he said.

Looking beyond optimal timing to begin screening, Wilt also discussed when it may be appropriate for patients to “focus on some other things” as they get older, highlighting a decreasing risk of developing cancer and benefiting from screening decrease with age.

Read the full article here: https://www.hcplive.com/view/timothy-wilt-md-mph-what-age-should-patients-get-screened-for-colorectal-cancer-

Hear more from Wilt: https://www.hcplive.com/view/timothy-wilt-md-mph-discussing-colorectal-cancer-screening-options-recommended-acp

title: When is it TIME to STOP Colon Cancer Screening?
description:
Have you been told its time to stop colon cancer screening? Or do you wonder if you really need another colonoscopy, and think its time to stop having a colonoscopy?

In this video, I discuss how we decide when it is time to stop colon cancer screening. First, its important to understand the goal of a colonoscopy - to prevent colon cancer. And that is done by removing polyps that may turn into colon cancer in the future. Second, I talk about when polyps may become cancer. Third, I explain why only having one colonoscopy isnt enough and if stool based colon cancer screening is ok. Fourth, I discuss how GI doctors determine how frequent your colonoscopies should be based on how many polyps or what type of polyps you have. Fifth, I eplain why someone would want to stop having colon cancer screening and what the guidlines state as a reasonable timeframe. Additionally, i talk about where the guidlines are not clear and how you and your doctor can explore when is the best time for you to stop screening. While a colonoscopy has many benefits, there are risks for people who have severe conditions and may not be the right choice for people with other comorbidities. So discuss these factors with your doctor!

title: Screening Guidelines for Those With a Family History of Colon Cancer
description:
Many who have a loved one with colon cancer wonder what their risk level is. It is no secret that if you have a family history of colon cancer you should be screened early and often. However, many people aren't sure if they are the right age or are just scared of what a colonoscopy might entail. Some people are scared that maybe cancer will  be found and avoid screening at all costs. Reasons like these are why early screening is such a big part of most colon cancer awareness efforts. Often, people just don't know that colon cancer doesn't have many symptoms until it is in advanced stages.

title: Colon Cancer Risk Factors: What You Need to Know from Boston Medical Center Expert
description:
HealthDay Interview with Jennifer Davids, MD, Chief of Colon and Rectal Surgery , Boston Medical Center

https://www.healthday.com/healthday-tv/cancer/colon-cancer-is-on-the-rise-in-young-adults-what-you-need-to-know


Colorectal cancer is now one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths among younger adults, prompting the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force to lower the recommended age for screening from 50 to 45. According to Dr. Jennifer Davids, Chief of Colon and Rectal Surgery at Boston Medical Center, colorectal cancer is increasingly affecting individuals in their 20s, 30s, and 40s. Many younger patients mistakenly attribute their symptoms to stress or diet, leading to late-stage diagnoses and more invasive treatments.

Symptoms of colorectal cancer can be subtle and mistaken for other conditions. Dr. Davids highlights changes in bowel habits, such as frequency, consistency, difficulty passing stools, urgency, and the presence of blood in the stool, as key warning signs. Additional symptoms include abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and changes in eating habits. Recognizing these signs early and seeking medical evaluation is crucial.

To protect oneself from colorectal cancer, screening is essential. "45 is the new 50," Dr. Davids emphasizes, urging individuals to stay on top of their screenings. Knowing one’s family history is also critical, as a history of polyps or colorectal cancer significantly increases risk. Many patients are unaware of their family history or hesitant to inquire, but understanding this information can guide screening decisions.

Colonoscopy remains the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening. While concerns about the invasiveness of the procedure or preparation process may deter some individuals, Dr. Davids stresses that any form of screening is better than none. Colonoscopy has the advantage of identifying and removing polyps and early-stage cancers in a single session, making it an effective preventative measure.

Lifestyle factors may also play a role in colorectal cancer prevention. Recent studies suggest that yogurt and calcium intake may contribute to a reduced risk. Dr. Davids explains that gut bacteria composition may influence inflammation and cancer development, though more research is needed to determine the extent of dietary impact.

Aspirin has also been studied for its potential in preventing the recurrence of colorectal cancer and polyps. While it is inexpensive and widely available, aspirin can cause gastrointestinal irritation and ulcers. Therefore, Dr. Davids advises individuals to consult their healthcare providers before taking aspirin as a preventive measure.

Given the rising rates of colorectal cancer in younger generations, spreading awareness is critical. Dr. Davids believes in normalizing conversations about bowel health, polyps, and colonoscopies. Public figures sharing their screening experiences on social media and news platforms can help reduce stigma and encourage proactive health measures. Looking out for peers and family members by promoting awareness and early screening can make a significant difference in reducing colorectal cancer mortality.

description:
When should I get screened for colon cancer? What is my risk if a relative was diagnosed at an age younger than 50? How can such a young and physically fit person like actor Chadwick Boseman die from this disease at the age of 43?

These are some of the common questions being raised worldwide with the shocking death of Black Panther star, Mr. Boseman. Primary care physicians and cancer specialists are fielding more questions than ever about colon cancer risk factors, symptoms and screening guidelines since the news broke of the actor’s death.

“The passing of this Hollywood star, Chadwick Boseman, has left me looking at him as a role model for our youth today, a role model to bring awareness to colorectal cancer,” says Sarah Joseph, M.D., medical oncologist at Miami Cancer Institute, with a focus on gastrointestinal cancers.

Sarah Joseph, M.D.:
As a GI, a gastroenterologist, oncologist at the Miami Cancer Institute I treat colorectal cancer. And a lot of my patients are under the age of 50 at time of diagnosis. All our screening has been geared towards a population age of over 50 years. So in that general population, in the above 50 to about 74 years old, that incidence of colorectal cancer has been decreasing. And that is predominantly because of increasing in screening, which are colonoscopies. The incidence in the age group less than 50 has been increasing. It has increased, I would say about 13%. title: Mayo Clinic Minute - Tips to make colonoscopy bowel prep easier
description:
For many people, one of the most uncomfortable parts of a colonoscopy is the preparation for the procedure.

The purpose of a colonoscopy is to examine the colon and rectum for abnormalities such as polyps, tumors or inflammation, aiding in the detection and prevention of colorectal cancer. And to do that, it's important your medical team has a clear view. 

Dr. Derek Ebner, a Mayo Clinic gastroenterologist, offers tips on how to make colonoscopy bowel prep, essentially a strong laxative, easier.

transcript_text: The entire spirit of doing the colonoscopy prep is to make sure that there is nothing in the colon. That's so your medical team can detect and remove polyps or lesions, says Mayo Clinic's Dr. Derek Ebner. We frequently hear that the colon preparation can be a challenge. Review your prep guidelines 1 to 2 weeks before your procedure for any special instructions. You may be encouraged to make small changes in your diet starting a week before the procedure. Often, the day before the colonoscopy is when you'll start the bowel prep solution. Dr. Ebner says this is where people may struggle. There's a couple of tricks. Often, you know, cooling the solution, drinking it through a straw can be helpful. Others like to have a small lime or a lemon wedge that they just bite into after doing some of the solution. Chewing gum also may help. And he says taking the solution is often spread out over 2 days, and that can help, too. Half of the volume is done the day before the procedure. The other half is done the day of the procedure. That helps make it a lot more tolerable, and in fact, we get a better cleanout by doing that splitting. For the Mayo Clinic News Network, I'm Jason Howland.

For your colonoscopy, your healthcare provider has identified a need for a preparation called Go Lightly. You can pick it up at the pharmacy and it will be called in for you. You will also have a flavor packet that's included when you pick it up from the pharmacy. 5 days before your procedure, you're going to hold all vitamins, iron, fiber supplements, and herbal products. Keep taking all heart and blood pressure medications. Do not stop those medications. You can continue taking your aspirin. There is no need to stop that medication. And if you need to take any pain or anti-inflammatory medications, you can take those as well. If you're diabetic, speak to your healthcare provider about your diabetes medication. You will definitely not take it the day of your procedure. You also may need adjustment to your dosages depending on what you take. So, talk to your prescribing healthcare provider. If you take a blood thinner, you're going to need to speak to your prescribing healthcare provider ahead of time to find out how many days before your procedure, you're going to need to stop taking that blood thinner. This is very important conversation that needs to be had. Up until this point, you've been able to eat a normal diet. But now, two days before your procedure, I want you to start on what's called a low residue diet. Foods that are low residue break down very easily and do not leave a lot of stool behind in the colon. Examples would be things like chicken, fish, rice, eggs, mashed potatoes. Things I want you to stay away from are things like fruit, and vegetables. They have a lot of fiber in them, and they're very slow to break down. Also, red meat, nuts, seeds, all of those things leave a lot of residue behind in the colon. The day before your procedure, you're going to need to start on a clear liquid diet. And when I say clear, that means not cloudy. So, you can still have dark things like coffee. You can have dark beef bullion, dark sodas, just nothing that's going to cloud it up. So, you cannot have any cream in any of these products or dairy because that clouds the product. So you can have coffee but no cream, no chunks of anything uh in any of these products. Just clear seeth through. Do not consume any red or purple products. And the reason for this is because your colon becomes a straight pipe. Whatever color you drink is similar to what is going to come out. So if you drink red, it looks like blood. So that's why we want you to avoid any red or purple products during this preparation time. If you drink just straight coffee and tea, you might be hungry. So, you may want to have a variety of things that can keep you satisfied. Sodium is good for that. So, you may want to have some clear chicken broth or beef broth because sometimes your body is craving sodium. description: This is What Happens During a Colonoscopy #pain. A colonoscopy is a crucial diagnostic procedure recommended for various indications, playing a pivotal role in preventive healthcare and early detection of colorectal issues. This endoscopic examination involves the insertion of a flexible tube equipped with a camera through the rectum into the colon, allowing for a detailed visual inspection of the colon's lining. Here are some key indications for undergoing a colonoscopy: Screening for Colorectal Cancer: Perhaps the most well-known indication, colonoscopies are recommended for routine screening to detect colorectal cancer in its early stages. Regular screenings are especially vital for individuals with a family history of colorectal cancer or those over the age of 50, as the risk of developing colorectal cancer increases with age. Polyp Detection and Removal: Colonoscopies enable the identification and removal of polyps, which are abnormal growths on the colon lining. Polyps can potentially develop into cancer over time, making their early removal a preventive measure against colorectal cancer. Evaluation of Gastrointestinal Symptoms: Persistent gastrointestinal symptoms such as unexplained abdominal pain, changes in bowel habits, rectal bleeding, or unexplained weight loss may necessitate a colonoscopy to investigate potential underlying issues, including colorectal conditions. Screening for Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD): Colonoscopies are instrumental in diagnosing and monitoring conditions like Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, both of which fall under the umbrella of inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD). Anemia Investigation: In cases of unexplained anemia, particularly when other diagnostic tests fail to identify the cause, a colonoscopy may be recommended to explore potential gastrointestinal bleeding or colorectal issues. Follow-up for Previous Colorectal Issues: Individuals with a history of colorectal conditions or surgeries may undergo colonoscopies as part of their ongoing monitoring and follow-up care. Evaluation of Unexplained Weight Loss: Unexplained weight loss can be a red flag for various health concerns, including colorectal issues, prompting the need for a thorough examination such as a colonoscopy. Diagnostic Tool for Other Gastrointestinal Conditions: Colonoscopies may be performed as a diagnostic tool to investigate and assess various gastrointestinal conditions beyond colorectal cancer, such as diverticulitis or ischemic colitis. In conclusion, a colonoscopy serves as a versatile and invaluable diagnostic tool, playing a pivotal role in preventive care and the early detection of colorectal issues. Hello, my name is Deanna and I am an anesthesia provider here at The Everett Clinic. I'm here to provide you with a brief overview of the sedation that you may receive for your colonoscopy and/or endoscopy. This video is meant as an introduction. You'll have an opportunity to speak in person with your gastroenterologist and sedation nurse immediately before your procedure to ask questions or discuss concerns that you may have. Most people undergoing colonoscopy and/or endoscopy will receive sedation through their IV. Many people do not remember having their procedure because of the sedation given. 

Some people don't even remember talking with their gastroenterologist but rest assured your doctor will give you written instruction and the results of your exam so that you have that information available once your sedation wears off. If you wish to be more awake or more asleep for your procedure then please let your nurse and physician know so they can adjust the amount of sedation to better match your wishes. Common drugs used are Propofol, Midazolam and occasionally Fentanyl. If you have allergies or concerns about what medicine will be used then please tell your nurse and physician when they meet you prior to your procedure. For most people, the sedation wears off quickly and you'll feel mostly back to normal within an hour or two. While you may feel normal, we instruct people to refrain from driving or making critical decisions for the remainder of the day. following your sedation as some people may still feel slightly impaired without realizing it.

transcript_text: [Music] How does colonoscopy sedation work? Imagine lying comfortably on a table, feeling relaxed and at ease while a doctor gently examines your colon. That's the power of sedation during a colonoscopy. Sedation helps make this important screening process more tolerable and less stressful. It works by using medications that relax your body and mind so you can stay comfortable throughout the procedure. There are two main types of sedation used for colonoscopies. The most common is conscious sedation also called moderate sedation. In this approach, a combination of a sedative and a pain reliever is given through an intravenous line. The sedative often a medication like mazzelam helps you relax and reduces anxiety. The pain reliever such as fentinil minimizes discomfort. With conscious sedation, you remain as awake but very relaxed. You might not remember much afterward, but you can respond to simple instructions if needed. Usually, a doctor and nurse manage this process without the need for an anesthesiologist. The second type is deep sedation, sometimes called monitored anesthesia care. This involves using a drug called Propole, which acts quickly to put you into a sleep-like state. An anesthesiologist or specially trained nurse administers the medication. When under deep sedation, most patients do not remember the procedure at all and sleep through the exam. Recovery from deep sedation is usually quick with many feeling alert within half an hour after the medication is stopped. This type of sedation offers a higher level of comfort, but requires closer monitoring of vital signs such as breathing and blood pressure. The choice between conscious and deep sedation depends on several factors. Your doctor will consider your medical history, any existing health conditions, and your personal preferences. The policies of the medical facility also play a role. Before the procedure, your health care provider will discuss these options with you to determine what is safest and most suitable for your situation. Sedation plays a crucial role in making colonoscopy a more acceptable and less intimidating experience. This is especially important because colonoscopies are a key tool for preventing colon cancer. During the procedure, doctors can remove polyp, which are growths that can turn into cancer if left untreated. Detecting and removing these early helps prevent colon cancer from developing. That's why sedation is a standard part of colonoscopy in many countries, aligning with guidelines from major health organizations. While sedation is generally safe, there are some risks. These can include drowsiness, temporary memory loss, or very rarely changes in breathing or heart rate. These risks are low when the procedure is performed by trained professionals in a properly equipped setting. Afterward, you will need someone to drive you home because the effects of sedation can impair your ability to operate a vehicle or make important decisions for several hours. It's very important to discuss any concerns with your doctor before the procedure. Let them know if you have reactions to anesthesia, sleep apneoa, or other health issues. This helps ensure your safety and comfort. Always follow your health care provers instructions before and after the colonoscopy. In summary, colonoscopy sedation works by carefully administering medications that keep you relaxed and painfree during the exam. This approach helps make screening more accessible and less frightening, supporting early detection and prevention of colon cancer. transcript_text: [Music] Can you skip a skin cancer screening if you have no symptoms? Many people wonder if they can skip a skin cancer check if they feel fine and see no issues. The truth is for most adults without any skin concerns or risk factors, routine skin exams by a doctor are not always necessary. Major health organizations, including the United States Preventive Services Task Force, say there is not enough evidence to recommend everyone get regular skin checks if they have no symptoms. This means that if you have no signs of skin problems and no personal or family history of skin cancer, skipping a screening is generally okay. However, it's important to understand that risk factors do matter. If you have a family history of melanoma, many atypical moles, very fair skin, or have spent lots of time in the sun, you might benefit from regular skin exams. People with these risk factors often see dermatologists once a year or more frequently to catch any early signs of trouble. Even if you are not in a high-risisk group, doing regular self-examinations can help. Learning to spot warning signs using simple rules like the absidity method can make a big difference. Look for asymmetry, irregular borders, multiple colors, a diameter larger than 6 mm, or changes over time. If you notice anything unusual, it's best to see a health care professional promptly. Remember, if you see a new or changing spot or if something looks different from your usual skin, don't ignore it. Symptoms like bleeding, itching, or pain should also prompt a visit to your doctor. While some organizations suggest periodic skin checks for adults over 20, especially those with risk factors, others prefer a more cautious approach due to limited evidence supporting routine screening for everyone. In the end, whether to have a professional skin exam depends on your personal risk and skin health. Staying aware of your skin's condition through self- exams and consulting a health care provider if you notice anything unusual is key. For those at higher risk, regular screenings can help catch skin cancer early when it is most treatable. Always talk with your health care provider to determine what's best for your individual situation. Remember, early detection saves lives and helps keep your skin healthy and vibrant.

transcript_text: Imagine you feel completely healthy and vibrant, but a hidden health concern could be silently impacting your well-being. This is a crucial area where being proactive can make all the difference, not just for you, but for others as well. You absolutely should get tested for sexually transmitted diseases or STDs, even if you do not have any symptoms. Many common STDs often present without noticeable signs, making regular testing an essential part of maintaining your sexual health. The primary reason for this is the asymptomatic nature of many infections. Diseases like clamidia, gorrhea, and even early stages of HIV can exist in your body for weeks, months, or sometimes even years without causing any outward symptoms. This means you could be unknowingly carrying an infection, risking your own long-term health and potentially transmitting it to sexual partners. Without symptoms, an STD can silently lead to serious health complications over time. For women, untreated clamidia or gorrhea can result in pelvic inflammatory disease or PID, which can cause chronic pelvic pain and even infertility. For men, these infections can lead to epidommitis affecting fertility. In treated HIV, of course, progresses to a IDS, while syphilis can cause severe organ damage in its later stages. Getting tested when you have no symptoms is a powerful act of self-care and responsibility towards your partners. It helps with early detection, allowing for timely treatment that can prevent serious health issues for you. Furthermore, it helps interrupt the chain of transmission, protecting your current and future partners from unknowingly contracting an STD. Many health care providers recommend annual STD screenings for sexually active individuals or more frequently if you have new or multiple partners. Think of STD testing as a routine health checkup much like getting a physical or a dental cleaning. It is a fundamental part of comprehensive sexual wellness. Early detection through testing means that treatments are often simpler and more effective, minimizing potential long-term impacts on your health and helping you maintain peace of mind in your relationships. >> [music]

title: No STD Symptoms? Why You Still Need to Get Tested
description:
Think you can't have an STD if you don't have symptoms? Think again. In this video, our Klinik Temasya doctor breaks down the silent nature of sexually transmitted diseases, why window periods matter, and what to expect during a screening. Learn how to protect your health, prevent long-term complications like Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID), and normalize sexual health checkups. transcript_text: Most people think that if they don't have any pain, itching, or strange symptoms, they are completely free from sexually transmitted diseases. They are completely wrong. In fact, relying on symptoms could put your long-term health at serious risk. Here's what most people don't know about these infections. Many of them are completely silent. By the end of this video, you will know exactly when you actually need to get tested and why what you don't feel can still hurt you. Let me explain what's actually going on. Sexually transmitted diseases or STDs are incredibly common worldwide. Infections like chlamyia, gorrhea, syphilis, and HPV spread through intimate contact. Because of the stigma, people avoid the clinic, allowing the infections to spread silently. A very common misconception in Malaysia is that you can only get an STD from standard intercourse. Actually, diseases like gorrhea and herpes are easily transmitted through oral sex, and HPV can spread just through intimate skin-to-skin contact. Condoms are great, but they don't protect against everything. For women, an untreated STD can travel up the reproductive tract, causing pelvic inflammatory disease. This leads to chronic deep pelvic pain, pain during intimacy, and severe scarring. Over time, this scarring can block the fallopian tubes, which is a major cause of infertility. In men, untreated infections can cause inflammation in the tubes at the back of the testice called epidommitis or affect the prostate gland. This causes painful urination, pelvic pain, and if left untreated for too long can also lead to blockages and male infertility. Beyond the physical symptoms, the psychological toll is huge. The physical pain during intimacy combined with the anxiety of transmitting an infection often leads to immense relationship stress and a loss of sexual confidence. I want you to know you don't have to suffer in silence. The good news is that many common STDs like chlamyia and syphilis are easily curable with a simple course of antibiotics from your doctor. Others like HIV or herpes are currently incurable but can be highly managed with modern medicine allowing you to live a perfectly normal life. Now, here is a crucial medical fact. Timing your test matters. Every STD has a window period. If you rush to the clinic and test too early after an exposure, your body hasn't produced the antibodies yet. This can give you a false negative result. Because of this window period, you must be honest with your doctor about when the exposure happened. We recommend regular screening at least once a year if you are sexually active or immediately if you have a new partner regardless of whether you feel symptoms. Having the talk with your partner can feel awkward but it is deeply necessary. In Malaysia, HIV testing is required for premarital screening, but I strongly advise couples getting married to also do a comprehensive STD screening for chlamyia, syphilis, and hepatitis as well. To protect yourself, use barrier methods correctly every single time. Also, make sure you get vaccinated. The HPV and hepatitis B vaccines are highly effective and widely available at clinics and hospitals across the country. Prevention is always better than cure. We need to normalize STD screening just like checking your cholesterol or blood pressure. It is a normal part of your overall healthcare. At the clinic, we just need a simple blood test, a urine sample, or a quick swab. It is fast and strictly confidential. If you do test positive, please don't panic. Having an STD doesn't make you a bad person. It simply means you caught an infection that needs treating. Our doctors at clinic Tamasha are here to help you get the right treatment without any judgment. Remember, regular screening is the only way to know your health status for sure. This video is for educational purposes only. Please consult your doctor or visit your nearest clinic for personalized medical advice. title: Myth vs. Fact: Do You Need Colon Cancer Screening Without Symptoms?
description:
Colon cancer symptoms are not always present, and that’s where this myth can be harmful. One of the most common misconceptions about colon cancer screening is the belief that you only need to screen if something feels wrong.

Fact: Colon cancer does not always cause symptoms, especially in its earlier stages¹. Many people with colorectal cancer feel completely fine, which means waiting for symptoms to appear can delay diagnosis. That’s why timely screening is important, even if you feel healthy. Screening is designed to help identify colorectal cancer or precancerous changes before symptoms develop, when treatment options may be more effective¹.

In this video, we break down:
• Why colon cancer can be present without noticeable symptoms
• Why symptoms are not a reliable signal for when to screen
• How screening fits into taking a proactive approach to your health

If you’ve been putting off colon cancer screening because you feel fine, this video is an important reminder: colon cancer doesn’t always send warning signs. 

Learn more about whether the Cologuard test may be right for you:  https://www.cologuard.com/is-cologuard-right-for-me
Learn more about colon cancer screening:  https://www.cologuard.com

#Cologuard #ColonCancerAwareness #ColonCancerScreening #GutCheck #ExactSciences #MythVsFact #ScreeningMatters #TimelyScreening

Important Note: Cologuard is not for everyone. If you’re experiencing symptoms or are at high risk for colon cancer, talk to your doctor about other screening options. 
 
Indication for Use: The Cologuard test is intended to screen adults 45 and older at average risk for colorectal cancer. Do not use if you have had adenomas, have inflammatory bowel disease, certain hereditary syndromes, or a personal or family history of colorectal cancer. Cologuard® is not a replacement for colonoscopy in high-risk patients. Cologuard performance in adults ages 45-49 is estimated based on a large clinical study of patients 50 and older. False positives and false negatives can occur. Rx only. Results may vary.

References: 
 ¹ Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Reducing Risk for Colorectal Cancer. Updated February 26, 2025. https://www.cdc.gov/colorectal-cancer/prevention/index.html

title: Colon cancer often has no symptoms.Screening saves lives.
description:
Colon cancer can develop silently.
Many patients have no symptoms in early stages.

By the time bleeding, weight loss, anemia, or bowel habit changes appear, the disease may already be advanced.

Who should get screened?

✔️ Everyone above 45 years
✔️ Earlier if there is family history
✔️ Patients with long-standing inflammatory bowel disease
✔️ Those with unexplained anemia

Screening options:

• Colonoscopy (gold standard)
• Stool-based tests (FIT test)
• CT colonography (in selected cases)

Early-stage colon cancer is highly treatable.
Late-stage disease requires more complex treatment.

Screening detects:
• Cancer early
• Pre-cancerous polyps before they turn into cancer

You may feel healthy.
That does not mean screening is unnecessary.

title: Screening for polyps and colon cancer
description:
Bowel cancer screening is one of the most effective ways to detect problems early—but it can also cause understandable concern and confusion. In this video, we explain the facts clearly and calmly, so you can make sense of what screening means for you.

In the UK, screening is offered using the Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) between the ages of 50 and 74. This simple at-home stool test looks for tiny, invisible traces of blood (occult blood) that may come from the lining of the bowel.

A positive FIT result does not mean cancer. It simply acts as a filter, identifying individuals who would benefit from a more definitive examination of the bowel—such as a colonoscopy or a less invasive colon capsule endoscopy.

It’s important to keep this in perspective.

As we get older, bowel polyps become quite common. However:
* The majority of polyps are small (less than 10mm)
* Most do not contain cancer or precancerous change
* Many are entirely harmless and may never cause problems

The focus of screening is to identify the small group of larger polyps, which are more likely to carry a risk of progression over time. These are the polyps that require priority assessment and removal, usually via colonoscopy, to prevent future cancer development.

In this video, we cover:

* How the FIT test works and why it is used
* What a positive (or negative) result really means
* The difference between small and large polyps
* Why most findings are low risk
* How screening helps prevent bowel cancer, not just detect it

Our aim is to provide balanced, evidence-based reassurance, helping you understand both the value of screening and the reality behind the results.

Screening is not about alarm, it’s about early detection, prevention, and peace of mind.

March is National Colorectal Cancer Awareness Month

Dr. Kyle Barnett with Granite Peaks Gastroenterology and Ron Fuller a colorectal cancer screening advocate talk more about the significance of raising awareness of the disease.

When men and women are combined, colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer deaths.

transcript_text: What happens if a polyp is found during your colonoscopy? Imagine sitting in the doctor's office hearing that during your colonoscopy a small growth called a polyp was found. What does that mean for your health? Well, during a colonoscopy doctors carefully examine your colon using a flexible tube called a colonoscope. If they spot a polyp, they usually remove it right then and there through a process called polypectomy. This is a key step in preventing colorectal cancer. The removal depends on the size and type of the polyp. Small polyps, usually less than a half inch, are often taken out with a wire loop that snips the polyp without using heat. This is called cold snare polypectomy. For medium-sized polyps, the doctor might use a wire loop with electrical current to cut and cauterize the tissue at the same time, known as hot snare polypectomy. Larger or flatter polyps might need a different approach, like injecting fluid underneath to lift them from the colon wall before removal, a technique called endoscopic mucosal resection. title: What happens after polyp biopsy?
description:
Learn more about colonoscopy at http://www.YouAndColonoscopy.com  
If a polyp or other abnormality is found during your colonoscopy, it will be removed by a biopsy or polypectomy, and the sample will be sent to a lab for analysis. In this video, Dr. Echavarria and Dr. Gelrud explain that a specially trained doctor (known as a pathologist) will closely examine the sample to check for signs of cancer or pre-cancer. It may take 1-2 weeks to receive the results of the biopsy from your doctor. A benign (non-cancer) result means that your risk of cancer is zero. However, many polyps that get removed do carry a low risk of turning into cancer. If the tissue sample is pre-cancerous you will need to meet with your doctor again. If you had pre-cancerous polyps removed it is good news, since you no longer have those polyps in your body. Patients who have polyps have a higher risk of developing more polyps in the future, so be sure to talk with your doctor about when your repeat colonoscopy should be scheduled.

description:
Michael F. Driscoll, M.D., medical oncologist answers the question, once colon cancer is diagnosed, what are the next steps?

For cancers that seem local/regional meaning contained in one area potentially maybe there's some lymph nodes that look suspicious on the CT scan but no evidence of any spread to let's say the liver or the lungs which would be more of a distant spread and denote a late stage such as stage four.

It's usually stage 1, 2, 3 we would go for surgery as the first option and surgery is really your best chance of cure.

Oftentimes the final stage is not known until the pathology comes back. Sometimes we would look at a colon cancer and say this looks relatively early stage maybe this is a stage one, potentially a stage 2 and we may get the pathology back which shows that the cancer has maybe invaded deeper into the colon or maybe in the pericolorectal tissues which are just outside of the colon or has maybe spread to the lymph nodes and if that's the case then that changes what we're going to do after the surgical resection.

As a general rule with the different stages of colon cancer typically stage 1 people just need a surgical resection and that is generally curative.

Stage 2 depending on your risk factors you may need chemotherapy after the fact.

Stage 3 tends to involve the lymph nodes and we know from clinical trials that people that have lymph node involvement with colon cancer definitively benefit from chemotherapy it decreases their risk of recurrence gives them a better overall survival.

So, those folks definitively need chemotherapy and then stage 4 is spread outside in the colon so it's a distant platastocyst or spread somewhere else most often times its to the liver. 

Colon cancer’s a little bit different cancer than some of the other solid tumor malignancies. When we look at other cancers such as let’s say pancreatic cancer or Cholangiocarcinoma which is a cancer of the biliary tract maybe even with cancer that starts in the liver and then spreads somewhere else, cellular carcinoma, or even lung cancer or breast cancer that tend to be stage four meaning distant metastasis oftentimes these are very difficult to cure.

Colon cancer is a little bit different in that when folks present with a single isolated metastasis or cancer to the liver from the colon and there's no evidence of any spread anywhere else we can still cure some of the stage 4 colon cancers with surgical resection or ablation of the liver metastases in addition to the chemotherapy.

title: Your Colon Cancer Stage Explained: Treatment Options & Survival Rates
description:
Understanding your stage of colon cancer can be the difference between confusion and clarity — between fear and a plan. In this video, I break down the colon cancer staging system (Stages 0 to IV) in simple terms, explain how staging is determined, and most importantly — how it affects treatment options, prognosis, and survival rates.

This video will give you a clear roadmap of what each stage means and why early detection saves lives.

transcript_text: When someone hears you have colon cancer, one of the first questions is what stage is it? Stage isn't just a label. It determines treatment plan and your chance of survival. Today, I'll break down how colon cancer staging works, what treatments go with each stage, and why catching it early matters so much. How staging works. The TNM system simplified. Colon cancer is staged based on the TNM system. T stands for the depth of tumor in the colon wall. N stands for lymph node involvement. M stands for metastasis meaning spread to other organs. These combine into stages 1 through four. Stage one is can cancer limited to the inner layers of the colon. Stage two is cancer that has grown through the wall but not to the lymph nodes. Stage three cancer has reached nearby lymph nodes. Cancer stage four cancer has spread to distant organs like liver or lungs. Check out our video using the TNN classification using the NCTCN guidelines as well. Staging tells doctors two key things. How aggressive treatment needs to be and what your outlook or prognosis might be. Someone with stage one cancer might only need surgery, while someone with stage three usually needs surgery plus chemotherapy. For stage four, treatment may focus on controlling disease and improving survival with a combination of surgery, chemo, and sometimes targeted therapies or immunotherapy. Without staging, we wouldn't know who needs what, and we might either undertreat or overtreat patients. Let's go through the treatments by stage. For stage one, surgery alone is usually curative. No chemotherapy. For stage two, surgery is standard. Some high-risk cases may get chemo. For example, if the tumor is large, perforated or poorly differentiated. Stage three surgery plus chemotherapy is standard. Chemo reduces the risk of recurrence by killing cancers left behind. Stage four treatment is more complex. Surgery may be done if the tumor is blocking the colon, but the main stay is systemic therapy, chemotherapy, targeted drugs like Bevacusimab and in selected patients immunotherapy. If cancer is limited to the lung or liver, sometimes surgery or ablation can still offer long-term survival. So what about survival? Staging also helps predict survival. According to the American Cancer Society's 2024 data, in stage one, the 5-year survival is about 90%. In stage two, it's about 75%. Stage three, it drops down to 55 to 60%. And for stage 4, it drops about down to 15%. So staging is not just medical jargon. It's about the roadmap for treatment and the single most important predictor of survival. If you're someone you know is facing colon cancer, understanding the stage helps make sense why certain treatments are recommended. To recap, colon cancer staging goes from stage 1 to four based on the tumor depth, lymph nodes, and spread. Each stage has a different treatment approach and survival outlook. title: Treatments for Colorectal Cancer
description:

MEDICAL ANIMATION TRANSCRIPT: 
Treatments for colorectal cancer include surgical procedures, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. Early cancer or polyps may be removed during a colonoscopy. During this procedure, a flexible tube will be inserted through your anus. In most cases, if a polyp is found, it will be removed. If a small area of cancer is found, it will be removed. For larger areas of cancer, you may need to have a surgical procedure to remove the affected part of your large intestine. Your surgeon may remove part of your colon, or part, or all of your rectum. Nearby tissue, such as lymph nodes may also be removed to see if cancer has spread there. In most cases, the remaining ends of your large intestine will be reattached. But, sometimes the surgeon will not attach the remaining ends right away. Instead, a procedure may be done to attach the top end of your large intestine to an opening in the skin of your abdomen and the bottom end will be closed with staples or sutures. This new opening in the skin allows solid waste to empty into an attached bag. Usually, the opening is temporary. If temporary, the ends of your large intestine will be reconnected in a later procedure. Chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or both may also be recommended, either before or after a surgical procedure. Chemotherapy uses drugs to attack and kill cancer cells. Radiation therapy is often used along with chemotherapy. The high energy rays in radiation therapy attack and destroy cancer cells. Other treatments may also be recommended for colorectal cancer. Talk to your healthcare provider if you have any questions.

The patient sometimes ask me if all of the
treatment is worth it after a diagnosis of colon cancer, so let's take a moment and talk
about what will happen if you don't get treated. Although early detection and treatment of
colon cancer is highly curable, stage IV cancer is almost always lethal. Before we have the newer chemotherapy drugs
in the natural course of the disease, we would quote a survival rate of about to six to eight
months for the patients with stage IV disease meaning cancer that has spread to other organs
if it went untreated. For an early stage patient who does not get
treated meaning the tumor is detected in the colon it might be in the lymph nodes, but
not in other organs yet, this time might depending on how aggressive the tumor is be extended
to a year or two, but invariably it is important for the patient to know that it will become
lethal. Now, colon cancer is a very special case because
it is so highly curable if you treat it early on and the treatment is usually very well
tolerated. The patients in their 90s are able to undergo
surgical resection with very good quality of life. There are support groups for the patient who
will end up with a bag. There is information about chemotherapies
and it is important to know that in the curative settings that means stage II and III colon
cancer where we give chemo only for six months. Most of the side effects, if you are treated
by experienced physician, will be gone within a few months to a couple of years. Some rare side effects such as numbness or
tingling caused by some of these chemotherapies occur if you take them for too long and your
physician does not pay attention and stop them in time. Otherwise, the patient should have an excellent
quality of life after curative treatment for colorectal cancer, so it is very important
to bring up your concerns with your physician specifically tell him what you are concerned
about and discuss the issues that I brought up. For an interactive tool to learn more about
your colon cancer and your personalized treatment options go to MyColonCancerCoach.org.
